source.title: Recent Results and Open Problems in Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization

accepted.question_text: Can multi-objective evolutionary algorithms, which evolve populations of candidate solutions to approximate trade-offs among several objectives, be designed around selection indicators other than hypervolume, such as inverted generational distance or Hausdorff-distance-style measures, so that selection remains computationally practical and still produces good Pareto-front approximations as the number of objectives increases?

evidence.quote: other performance measures as possible alternatives to the hypervolume.
other performance measures that could be used for selection but have not been explored

accepted.question_text: For expensive multi-objective optimization problems, where objective-function evaluations are costly, how can fitness approximation and surrogate modeling be incorporated into multi-objective evolutionary algorithms so that fewer true objective evaluations are needed without losing reliable approximation of the Pareto front?

evidence.quote: Taking this to the multiobjective case is not trivial
The implementation of MOEAs that incorporate surrogate methods is not trivial!

accepted.question_text: How should parallel multi-objective evolutionary algorithms be architected for expensive optimization problems: should they maintain local external archives or one global archive, can independent demes search non-overlapping regions of the search space, and can GPU-based implementations be made efficient and effective?

evidence.quote: should we use local external archives or only a global one?
What about GPU-based implementations

accepted.question_text: Can self-adaptive or online-adaptive multi-objective evolutionary algorithms be made effectively parameterless by automatically choosing parameters such as mutation rate, crossover rate, population size, or encoding while using well-defined convergence criteria and population-behavior signals to guide the search?

evidence.quote: dream of creating a parameterless multi-objective evolutionary algorithm
difficulty to define convergence criteria

accepted.question_text: What stopping criteria can reliably decide when a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm should terminate, so that parameterless MOEAs can stop based on convergence or lack of improvement rather than an externally fixed iteration budget?

evidence.quote: Another missing mechanism to get to a parameterless MOEA is a well-established stopping criterion.

accepted.question_text: How can multi-objective evolutionary algorithms scale to many-objective optimization, where Pareto-dominance-based selection loses pressure because nondominated solutions grow rapidly with the number of objectives, and where the number of solutions needed to sample the Pareto front also grows rapidly?

evidence.quote: MOEAs that adopt a selection mechanism based on Pareto optimality do not scale properly
the number of solutions required to sample the Pareto front, also grows exponentially.

accepted.question_text: How can multi-objective evolutionary algorithms scale in the decision-variable space, especially for problems with hundreds or thousands of decision variables, rather than only scaling in the number of objectives?

evidence.quote: What about scalability in decision variable space?
There is almost no work on this topic

accepted.question_text: Which structural features make a multi-objective optimization problem difficult for a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm, and which algorithmic features should a MOEA have to solve real-world problems or meaningful subclasses efficiently?

evidence.quote: What makes a problem difficult for a MOEA?
we do not know what features are desirable in a MOEA

accepted.question_text: What is the practical efficiency limit for multi-objective evolutionary algorithms: can algorithms that currently need fewer than about 5,000 objective-function evaluations for reasonable Pareto-front approximations be reduced to about 1,000 evaluations while preserving robust behavior, and what should robustness mean in a multi-objective setting?

evidence.quote: less than 5,000 objective function evaluations
Can we reduce this figure to 1,000?
What is robustness in a multi-objective context?

accepted.question_text: How can multi-objective evolutionary algorithms explicitly handle constraints in constrained multi-objective optimization problems, beyond simple changes to Pareto dominance rules, and what benchmark problems should be used to evaluate constraint handling fairly?

evidence.quote: very few approaches exist to explicitly handle constraints in multi-objective optimization problems.
current benchmarks adopted for testing new MOEAs

accepted.question_text: How can evolutionary algorithms be effectively hybridized with mathematical programming techniques, including game-theoretic methods, min-max optimality, or epsilon-constraint-style methods, to produce stronger multi-objective evolutionary algorithms?
accepted.context_brief: Hybrid evolutionary and mathematical programming methods

evidence.quote: underestimated the potential of hybridizing evolutionary algorithms with mathematical programming techniques.
game theory, min-max optimality, and the ε-constraint method

accepted.question_text: How should multi-objective evolutionary algorithms address uncertainty and dynamic change, including stochastic dominance, stochastic multi-objective combinatorial optimization, and dynamic multi-objective problems, where the objectives or environment may vary or be uncertain?

evidence.quote: stochastic dominance or stochastic multi-objective combinatorial problems
can give rise to new MOEAs

accepted.question_text: How can researchers visualize Pareto fronts in high-dimensional objective spaces so that decision makers can understand solution trade-offs produced by multi-objective evolutionary algorithms?

evidence.quote: visualization of a Pareto front in a high-dimensional space.

accepted.question_text: How can benchmark test problems for multi-objective evolutionary algorithms be designed so that they reflect the actual difficulties of real-world problems, rather than only artificial ZDT, DTLZ, Okabe, or WFG-style test suites?

evidence.quote: loosely related to the actual difficulties that real-world problems have.

accepted.question_text: What new algorithm, operator, or mechanism could become a third-generation idea for multi-objective evolutionary optimization, powerful enough for subsequent researchers to build on?

evidence.quote: This will probably be an algorithm, although it could be simply an operator or a specific mechanism.

trace.notes: Original input normalized as the zbMATH resolver URL https://zbmath.org/7631416.

Local shard metadata identified zbMATH record 7631416 as 'Recent results and open problems in evolutionary multiobjective optimization' with DOI 10.1007/978-3-319-71069-3_1. The Springer DOI page confirmed the same title, author Carlos A. Coello Coello, pages 3-21, and subscription-preview access only. Bounded exact-title recovery found a readable same-title same-author PDF deck at the Wellington ECRG site; that PDF was used as the readable extraction artifact.

Mapped the 67-page PDF deck. Section structure: Introduction; Recent Results and Open Problems with subsections Algorithms, MOEAs for Expensive Objective Functions, Self-Adaptation and Online Adaptation, and Scalability; The Challenges of this Century; Conclusions. Open-problem-bearing regions are pages 18-19, 26-29, 34-40, 50, and 54-63.
The Introduction pages provide terminology and historical context for MOEAs but no accepted standalone open-problem candidate.
Extracted one candidate on selection mechanisms based on performance measures other than hypervolume.
Extracted candidates on fitness approximation, surrogate methods, and parallel MOEA architecture for expensive objective functions.
Extracted candidates on parameterless self-adaptive MOEAs and stopping criteria.
Extracted candidates on many-objective scaling and scaling in decision-variable space.

Extracted candidates from The Challenges of this Century on sources of problem difficulty, efficiency and robustness, constraints, hybridization, uncertainty and dynamism, visualization, benchmarks, and third-generation mechanisms.
The Conclusions restate the need for more profound ideas and tailored algorithms but did not add a distinct candidate beyond the challenge items already extracted.
